definition: Imaging with electrons instead of light, sharp enough to see individual synapses; used to reconstruct connectomes.
A family of card games in which players bet on who holds the best hand, and can win without it by betting so that everyone else folds.
The most played form of poker: each player gets two hole cards and shares five community cards, dealt in a flop, turn and river, with four betting rounds.
The cards dealt face down to one player, seen only by them. Two in hold'em, four in Omaha.
Cards dealt face up in the middle of the table that every player uses in their hand. In hold'em there are five: the flop, turn and river.
The community cards on the table at any point in a hand, as in 'the board is K 7 2'.
The first betting round of a hold'em hand, after the hole cards are dealt and before any community cards.
The first three community cards in hold'em, dealt together, and the betting round after them. As a verb, to flop a hand is to make it with those cards.
The fourth community card in hold'em, and the betting round after it. Also called fourth street.
The fifth and last community card in hold'em, and the final betting round after it. Also called fifth street.
The end of a hand when two or more players remain after the last betting round: they show their cards and the best hand wins the pot.
The smaller of the two forced bets posted before the cards are dealt, by the player to the dealer's left (by the dealer, heads-up); usually half a big blind. Also the seat that posts it.
The larger forced bet, posted by the second player to the dealer's left before the cards are dealt. Stakes, stacks and win rates are measured in big blinds (bb).
A small forced bet taken from every player (or, as a big-blind ante, from one player for the whole table) before a hand, to make the pot bigger. Common in tournaments.
The disc marking the nominal dealer, who acts last after the flop. It moves one seat clockwise every hand. Also the seat itself, the best position at the table.
To decline to bet while keeping the hand, passing the action on. Only possible when nobody has bet on this round.
To match the current bet and stay in the hand.
To increase the current bet. Others must then match the larger amount, raise again or fold.
To give up a hand and any chips already put into the pot.
Having put every chip you have into the pot. A player all-in for less than a bet can only win that much from each other player; the rest goes to a side pot.
A separate pot made by the chips a short-stacked all-in player cannot match. Only the players who put chips into it can win it.
A pot shared equally between players whose hands tie exactly. Also called a chop.
The first raise of a hand before the flop, also called an open. Entering a pot by raising rather than calling is standard in modern play.
To enter the pot before the flop by just calling the big blind rather than raising. Mostly a sign of a weak player, except from the small blind.
A betting structure in which a player may bet any amount up to all their chips at any time.
A betting structure in which the largest bet or raise is the size of the pot, counting the call. The usual structure for Omaha.
A betting structure with bets and raises in fixed sizes: a small bet on the first two rounds and a big bet on the last two, usually capped at four bets per round.
A poker game played for chips worth real money, which players can join, leave and buy into at any time. Also called a ring game.
The chips a player has in front of them, usually measured in big blinds.
The order of poker hands from best to worst: royal flush, straight flush, four of a kind, full house, flush, straight, three of a kind, two pair, one pair, high card.
A-K-Q-J-T all of one suit: the best possible hand in standard poker, the highest straight flush.
Five cards in sequence, all of one suit. Only 40 of the 2,598,960 five-card hands, including the four royal flushes.
Four cards of the same rank, such as four queens. Also called quads.
Three cards of one rank and two of another. Ranked first by the three of a kind: kings full of fours beats queens full of aces.
Five cards of the same suit, not in sequence. Compared by the highest card, then the next.
Five cards of consecutive rank in more than one suit. The ace can play high (A-K-Q-J-T, Broadway) or low (5-4-3-2-A, the wheel).
Three cards of one rank. Made with a pocket pair and one board card it is a set; with one hole card and a pair on the board it is trips.
Two cards of one rank, two of another and a fifth card.
An unpaired side card that decides between hands of the same kind: with A-K against A-Q on an ace-high board, the king kicker wins.
5-4-3-2-A, the lowest straight; also the best hand in ace-to-five lowball.
The first seat to act before the flop, just left of the big blind. The worst position preflop, so it plays the fewest hands.
The seat to the right of the button, the second-best position at the table.
The seat two to the right of the button, before the cutoff.
The seat three to the right of the button, before the hijack. In six-handed games it is the first to act, often called UTG.
Acting after a given opponent on the flop, turn and river, an advantage on every street because you see their action first.
Acting before a given opponent on the flop, turn and river, which makes every decision harder.
A form of poker with four hole cards, of which a hand must use exactly two with exactly three community cards. Usually played pot-limit (PLO).
A form of poker with no community cards: each player gets seven cards of their own, some face up, over five betting rounds.
Forms of poker in which the lowest hand wins, such as ace-to-five (Razz) and deuce-to-seven (2-7 triple draw).

Split-pot poker in which the best high hand and the best qualifying low hand (five cards of different ranks, all eight or lower) each win half the pot; with no qualifying low, the high hand takes it all. Winning both halves is scooping.
Hold'em played with the 2s to 5s removed, leaving 36 cards, so a flush beats a full house. Also called six-plus hold'em.
One specific pair of hole cards, such as AhKd, often called a combo. There are 1,326 in all: 6 for each pocket pair, 4 for each suited hand and 12 for each offsuit hand.
The hole cards a player is dealt. Hold'em has 169 kinds of starting hand (13 pairs, 78 suited and 78 offsuit) made from 1,326 combinations.
Two hole cards of the same rank, such as 7-7. One hand in 17 is a pocket pair.
Of two hole cards: the same suit, written with an s (AKs). Suited hands can make flushes, worth a few percent of equity.
Of two hole cards: different suits, written with an o (AKo).
Suited hole cards of consecutive rank, such as 8-7 suited. They make straights and flushes and play well in deep-stacked pots.
The cards ten through ace, which make the highest straight (A-K-Q-J-T, Broadway).
The effect of the cards you can see on which combinations an opponent can hold: holding an ace leaves only three combos of AA.
A card in your hand that makes certain hands impossible or less likely for an opponent, such as the ace of the flush suit blocking the nut flush.
The unseen cards that would turn a hand that is behind into the best hand.
A shortcut for drawing odds: on the flop, outs times 4 is roughly the percentage chance of hitting by the river; on the turn, outs times 2 is the chance on the river.
Four cards of one suit, needing one more to make a flush: 9 outs, about 35% to get there from the flop to the river.
Four cards in a row that can be completed at either end, such as 8-7-6-5: 8 outs, about 31.5% from the flop.
A straight draw that needs one inside card, such as 9-8-6-5 needing a 7: 4 outs, about 16.5% from the flop. Also called an inside straight draw.
A hand with two draws at once, typically a flush draw with a straight draw. With 15 outs on the flop it is a slight favourite (about 54%) even against a made hand.
A draw that needs both the turn and river cards, such as a backdoor flush. Worth about one out: around 4% for a backdoor flush.
Three of a kind made with a pocket pair and one matching board card. A pocket pair flops a set or better about 11.8% of the time.
Three of a kind made with one hole card and a pair on the board. Weaker than a set, because the third card is easy for others to share.
A card higher than any on the board, or higher than a pocket pair. AK on a flop of 8-6-2 has two overcards, about 6 outs.
A pocket pair higher than every card on the board, such as QQ on J-7-3.
A pair made with the highest card on the board.
An all-in between two hands with close to equal equity, classically a pocket pair against two higher cards (22 against AK, about 53% to 47%).
A hand is dominated when it shares a card with a better hand, as AQ is with AK: it wins only about a quarter of the time.
A hand's share of the pot if it were played to the end with no more betting: its chance of winning plus half its chance of tying.
Losing a hand in which you were a big favourite when the money went in.
A hand in which a strong hand meets a stronger one and big losses are unavoidable, such as KK against AA preflop.
The ratio of the pot to the cost of a call. A call needs at least call / (pot after the call) equity to break even: 25% against a half-pot bet, 33% against a pot-sized one.
The average result of a decision over every way it could turn out, weighted by probability. Poker skill is choosing the action with the highest EV.
Pot odds that also count what you expect to win on later streets if your draw comes in. They justify calls with set-mining hands and draws when stacks are deep.
The extra you expect to lose on later streets when your hand improves to a second-best hand, such as a low flush against a higher one.
The part of a bet's value that comes from the opponent folding. Gives semi-bluffs and short-stack shoves their profit.
A bet or raise with a hand that is probably behind but can improve to the best hand, such as a flush draw. It wins when they fold and sometimes when called.
A bet or raise with a weak hand, meant to make better hands fold.
The break-even fold frequency of a bluff: a bet b into a pot p must work b / (p + b) of the time. A pot-sized bluff needs 50%.
The share of a range, p / (p + b), a player must continue with against a bet of b into a pot p so that a bluff can't profit automatically: 50% against a pot-sized bet.
The smaller of the stacks between two players, the most either can win or lose against the other.
The effective stack divided by the pot on the flop. Low SPR makes one-pair hands strong enough to commit; high SPR favours hands that can make the nuts.
Having so much of a stack in the pot that calling the rest is profitable with almost any equity, because of the pot odds, not the money already spent.
The fee the house takes from each pot, usually a percentage up to a cap. Rakeback returns some of it.
Calling with a small pocket pair mainly to flop a set, which happens about 1 time in 8.5. Pays only with enough implied odds.
Results with each all-in hand counted at its expected value when the money went in instead of its actual outcome, removing the luck of the run-out.
Where a player sits relative to the dealer button, and so when they act. Acting last is a big advantage; see in position and out of position.
The set of hands a player raises with when first into the pot from a given seat; it widens from about 15% under the gun to 40% or more on the button.
The first re-raise before the flop (the big blind counts as the first bet and the open as the second). Usually about 3 times the open in position and 4 times out of position.
A re-raise of a 3-bet, usually about 2.2 to 2.5 times its size. With 100 big blinds it often commits the player to the pot.
A 3-bet after an open and one or more callers, whose calls suggest hands too weak to 3-bet.
Calling a raise without any money already in the pot.
A bet on the flop by the player who made the last raise before it.
Checking, then raising after an opponent bets. A strong play out of position with very strong hands and semi-bluffs.
A bet into the player who was the aggressor on the previous street, from out of position. Also called a lead.
Calling a bet in position with a weak hand, planning to take the pot later when the opponent shows weakness.
A bet on the turn from out of position after the preflop aggressor checked behind on the flop.
A bet on a later street after betting the one before. Betting flop, turn and river is a triple barrel.
Checking or calling with a very strong hand to hide its strength and let the opponent bet or catch up.
Checking or calling with a medium-strength hand to keep the pot small.
A bet bigger than the pot, used with a polarised range when you hold more of the nuts than the opponent.
A bet made to get called by worse hands. A thin value bet is one only slightly ahead of the hands that call.
How a board's cards connect with each other and with likely hands: dry boards have few draws, wet (dynamic) boards many; paired and monotone boards change which hands are strong.
Betting the same fraction of the pot on each remaining street so that the stacks go in exactly by the river.
The chance a hand wins if the hand is checked down to showdown. Hands with showdown value often check rather than bet or bluff.
Adjusting to an opponent's mistakes to win more from them, at the cost of becoming exploitable yourself.
A player who plays few hands and plays them mostly by betting and raising. The usual winning style.
A player who plays many hands, aggressively.
A very tight player who plays few hands and rarely bluffs.
A player who calls too much and rarely raises or folds. Value-bet them thinly and don't bluff them.
A weak, usually recreational player.
A player who bets and raises with almost any hand.
Choosing which games to play by the weakness of the opponents in them, one of the biggest sources of a winning player's profit.
Software that shows statistics on each opponent at an online table, built from a database of past hands.
Voluntarily put money in pot: the share of hands in which a player calls or raises before the flop, not counting forced blinds. A measure of how loose they are.
Preflop raise: the share of hands a player raises before the flop.
After the flop, bets plus raises divided by calls. High numbers mean an aggressive player.
Went to showdown: the share of hands that saw the flop in which a player went to showdown. High numbers mark a calling station.
A behaviour that gives away information about a player's hand, such as acting fast, a change in posture or a pattern of bet sizes.
Playing worse because of emotion, usually after bad beats or losses.
Judging a decision by how it turned out instead of by its expected value.
Thinking about what an opponent thinks you hold, and what they think you think, and so on.
Every hand a player could hold in a spot, each weighted by how likely it is. Players read and plan in ranges, not single hands.
A range that mixes strong hands and bluffs (and protects its checks with some strong hands) in proportions that leave nothing to exploit.
A range of very strong hands and bluffs with few medium hands, suited to large bets.
A range of the strongest hands down to a cut-off, also called merged, suited to smaller bets that get called by slightly worse hands.
A range of mostly medium-strength hands, such as a calling range, which struggles against big bets.
A range that can't contain the strongest hands, because with them the player would have raised earlier.
Having more equity across your whole range than the opponent does across theirs on a given board. It favours betting often.
Having more of the very strongest hands than the opponent on a given board. It allows large bets and overbets.
The best possible hand given the board. The nut flush is the best possible flush.
A hand that beats only bluffs and loses to every value bet; its decision to call depends only on how often the opponent bluffs.
A poker strategy that is a Nash equilibrium (or close to one): it can't be exploited, so in two-player zero-sum games it loses nothing in expectation from a symmetric position against any opponent.
How much a perfect counter-strategy would win against a strategy. A Nash equilibrium has zero exploitability.
Playing the same hand in more than one way at set frequencies, such as betting 60% and checking 40%, as equilibrium strategies often do.
At equilibrium, a player mixes between two actions only when they have equal EV, and the opponent's frequencies are set to make them so. The source of equilibrium bluffing and calling frequencies.
A toy poker game with a three-card deck used to show equilibrium bluffing and calling: the bettor bluffs the queen one time in three and the caller calls with the king one time in three.
A simplified version of poker, small enough to solve by hand, used to show equilibrium ideas.
The share of its raw equity a hand actually wins, given the betting to come. In position and suited hands realise more; out of position and offsuit ones less.
A program that computes an approximate Nash equilibrium for a poker situation defined by ranges, board, stacks and allowed bet sizes.

An algorithm that finds approximate equilibria by self-play: it repeatedly shifts the strategy at every decision towards the actions it most regrets not taking. Its average strategy converges to a Nash equilibrium in two-player zero-sum games.
Fixing an opponent's strategy at one decision in a solver and computing the best response to it, to find exploitative adjustments.
Grouping similar hands, cards or bet sizes into one in order to make a game small enough to solve.
Sklansky's principle: whenever you play a hand differently from how you would if you could see the opponents' cards, they gain; whenever you play it the same way, you gain.
A poker event where everyone starts with equal chips, blinds rise on a schedule and players are knocked out; prizes go to the last few by finishing place.
A model that turns tournament stacks into shares of the prize pool by assuming each player finishes first with their share of the chips, then second among the rest in the same way, and so on.
The point in a tournament just before the paid places, when one more elimination puts every remaining player in the money.
The prize equity a player loses by losing an all-in, divided by what they gain by winning it. A bubble factor of 2 means an even-money all-in needs 67% equity.
The extra equity, above the chip-EV break-even, that ICM makes a tournament player need to call an all-in.
Expected value measured in tournament chips rather than prize money. Close to money EV early in a tournament, far from it near the money.
Expected value measured in prize money, the thing a tournament player wants to maximise; ICM estimates it from stacks.
The short-stack strategy of either going all in or folding, close to optimal below about 15 big blinds. Nash push-fold charts give the shoving and calling ranges.
Harrington's measure of a tournament stack: chips divided by the cost of one round of blinds and antes, the number of orbits a player could survive without playing.
The last table of a multi-table tournament, where the biggest prize jumps are.
A deal among the last players of a tournament that splits the remaining prize money by ICM equity. A chip chop splits by chip share instead, favouring the leader.
A bounty tournament in which half of a busted player's bounty goes to the eliminator at once and half is added to the eliminator's own bounty.
A tournament whose prizes are seats in a bigger tournament. Since every seat is worth the same, ICM pressure near the bubble is extreme.
A tournament that starts as soon as enough players have registered, often a single table.
A cash-game player's average profit, usually in big blinds per 100 hands (bb/100).
How widely a poker player's results swing, usually measured in big blinds per 100 hands. Typically 60 to 100 bb/100 in no-limit hold'em.
The swings of results around their expected value caused by luck. In poker it is large: winning players routinely lose for tens of thousands of hands.
A stretch of losing results. Downswings of 10 to 20 buy-ins are ordinary even for strong cash-game players.
The chance a bankroll is lost entirely before it grows. For win rate w, standard deviation s and bankroll B (in the same units) it is about exp(-2wB/s²) at fixed stakes.
The money set aside for playing poker, measured in buy-ins of the stake played.
Rules for which stakes to play for a given bankroll, such as keeping 20 to 50 buy-ins for cash games and many more for tournaments, to keep the risk of going broke low.
The amount a player pays to enter a tournament, or brings to a cash game; 100 big blinds is the usual cash-game buy-in.
A tournament player's profit divided by their total buy-ins.
The number of hands (or tournaments) behind a result or statistic. Poker needs large samples: about 100,000 hands narrow a win rate only to about plus or minus 6 bb/100.
The staking rule that maximises the long-run growth rate of a bankroll; it says to risk a small share of the bankroll when the edge is small relative to the variance.
Finished, or still playing, in a paid place of a tournament: past the bubble.
